column2: follow-up question (asked when this keyPoint is uncertain; must not contain the answer)
Sort food, a gaming console and a holiday abroad into needs and wants, and say what is special about wants over time.
Steel can make medical equipment, aircraft or refrigerators. What does that show about the choices a country faces?
What does the Greek root of 'economics' mean, and what kind of decisions does the subject study?
Why do economists rely on data, and in what fields do they work?
A student has money for a notebook or for saving towards a racket. What does choosing one cost the student, in economic terms?
What does a downward-sloping production possibility curve tell you about producing more of one good, and what do the points on it represent?
Why might a farmer who chooses a very profitable water-hungry crop be paying a hidden price, and what is that price called?
Why are shoes for students, for office workers and for athletes all different even though they are all footwear?
Compare how a handicraft workshop and a steel plant are staffed and equipped, and what each is called.
A garment factory owner finds machines have become much cheaper. What is likely to change, and what other things would affect that decision?
Who decides what, how much and for whom to produce when a central authority runs everything, and what is the downside for quality and innovation?
What forces decide production when private buyers and sellers lead, what role does the government keep, and why does competition help consumers?
Why do economists say that almost every real economy is a mixture, even those called market economies?
How did the way India ran its economy change after 1991, and what was it like before?
